strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored setting: personalized federated learning with simultaneous task, distribution, and architecture heterogeneity.
FedMosaic combines a similarity-aware aggregation mechanism with a dimension-independent adapter design, and DRAKE offers a broad evaluation across 40 multimodal tasks.

The empirical study is extensive, covering static and dynamic settings, multiple model families and sizes, LLM and multimodal benchmarks, per-client results, adaptation tests, and several component ablations.
FedMosaic generally improves cross-client generalization substantially and often improves personalization over both local fine-tuning and numerous recent baselines.
weaknesses: The mathematical specification of PQ-LoRA contains serious dimensional errors. For A in R^{r x d}, row orthogonality requires AA^T=I_r, yet Eqs. 22-23 incorrectly enforce A^T A=I, which is impossible when r<d. The stated full-SVD dimensions also make UV^T undefined. These errors directly affect the claimed alignment implementation.

The CCA-based B alignment is insufficiently sound: CCA projections are generally rectangular and non-invertible, but the method assumes an inverse; Eq. 21 also appears to use the wrong projection matrix. Moreover, a generic CCA transformation does not preserve orthogonality as claimed. These issues leave a central component ambiguous and potentially unreproducible.

Theorem 2 only proves zero aggregation error when every client has identical A and B. That assumption cannot hold across the heterogeneous architectures motivating the paper because their dimensions differ. The assertion that the result easily extends to heterogeneous models is unsupported, so the theory does not justify the central cross-architecture aggregation claim.

The incremental evidence for SIMA is weak and partly contradicts the prose: adding SIMA after PQ-LoRA slightly reduces some Others metrics in Table 5, while its dedicated ablation reports only Self performance. Thus, most of the observed benefit may come from PQ-LoRA, and the claimed generalization benefit of similarity-aware aggregation is not convincingly isolated.

SIMA requires clients to compute and apparently upload last-layer gradients from a shared auxiliary model. The paper does not account for this communication cost, quantify gradient dimensionality, compare communication volume, or evaluate gradient-based privacy leakage. This omission is important because privacy and efficiency motivate the work.

The realism claims are overstated: experiments use at most 10 clients, memory-infinite replay, only four sequential task blocks, and client architectures selected post hoc using supervised-fine-tuning performance. DRAKE is useful but is assembled from existing datasets rather than demonstrating deployment-scale federated heterogeneity. strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored setting: personalized federated learning with simultaneous task, distribution, and model-architecture heterogeneity.

DRAKE covers 40 tasks drawn from 19 multimodal datasets, and the evaluation spans static and dynamic settings, multiple model scales and families, LLM and MLLM benchmarks, numerous baselines, three seeds, ablations, and computational-cost analysis.

FedMosaic generally delivers consistent empirical gains, particularly on cross-client generalization, and the combination of similarity-aware aggregation with architecture-independent adapter parameters is intuitively appealing.
The main paper is clearly organized, and the appendix provides extensive benchmark and per-client results.
weaknesses: The central PQ-LoRA alignment procedure contains serious mathematical inconsistencies. CCA projection matrices are treated as invertible even though they are generally rectangular or singular; the main text and Eq. 21 use inconsistent projections; and an arbitrary CCA transformation does not preserve the claimed orthogonality of B.

The treatment of A is dimensionally invalid as written. For A in R^{r x d} with r<d, Eqs. 22-23 require A^T A=I, which is impossible because A^T A has rank at most r. The appropriate row-orthogonality condition would involve AA^T. The stated SVD dimensions also make UV^T undefined. These errors directly affect the method's initialization, theoretical justification, and reproducibility.

The pseudocode does not resolve these issues and introduces further ambiguities or errors: gradient frequency is conditioned on the client index rather than the iteration, several dimensions and variables are undefined, Algorithm 3 appears to update the entire model instead of only A, and Algorithm 4 applies an unspecified matrix inverse while inconsistently iterating over layers. No code is provided to establish what was actually implemented.

The experimental construction only weakly supports the claimed real-world setting. Distribution shifts are artificially produced by ordering manually defined task partitions, training assumes infinite episodic memory, experiments use at most ten clients, and model sizes are assigned post hoc according to task-specific SFT performance rather than genuine device constraints. This assignment procedure may also favor the proposed configuration.

The component evidence is weaker than claimed. Adding SIMA to PQ-LoRA slightly reduces several generalization results in Table 5, while the alignment improvements in Table 21 are small relative to their reported variability. There is no convincing isolation of the questionable CCA transformation, orthogonality enforcement, and blockwise correspondence assumptions.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility are insufficiently established. Several baselines are modified by combining them with Fed-ET, but these adaptations are not specified in enough detail, and relevant recent selective LoRA aggregation work cited by the paper is not evaluated. The benchmark and code are promised only after publication.

Privacy is used as a principal motivation, yet SIMA communicates task gradients and the method provides no threat model, formal privacy mechanism, or leakage evaluation. Sharing gradients and model updates is not inherently privacy-preserving.

Some evaluations need stronger validation: fast-adaptation curves lack uncertainty, the GPT-based Fed-Aya metric has no human agreement analysis, and exact-token scoring can be unreliable for open-ended multimodal answers. Overall, promising empirical results do not compensate for the unresolved technical validity and reproducibility problems in the core method.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored setting: personalized federated learning with simultaneous task/data heterogeneity, temporal distribution shifts, and heterogeneous client architectures.
FedMosaic combines two coherent ideas: SIMA for client-specific similarity-weighted aggregation and PQ-LoRA for sharing dimension-invariant parameters across models with different widths and depths.
DRAKE is a potentially valuable benchmark, covering 40 tasks from 19 datasets, multiple multimodal task families, distribution shifts, and unseen-task evaluation.

The empirical study is unusually broad: it includes DRAKE, HFLB, Fed-Aya, and Fed-LLM; static and dynamic settings; homogeneous and heterogeneous models; Llama- and Qwen-based variants; two- and three-model configurations; strong baselines; three seeds; efficiency analysis; and several component ablations.

FedMosaic consistently improves average personalization and especially cross-client generalization. The per-client results also show that both small and large models can benefit, while the fast-adaptation experiments support the usefulness of the learned shared knowledge.
The paper is generally well organized, and the main motivation, method components, and experimental conclusions are easy to follow.
weaknesses: The mathematical presentation of PQ-LoRA alignment contains serious dimensional inconsistencies. For A in R^{r×d}, row orthogonality requires AA^T=I_r, but Eq. 22 and Eq. 23 instead use A^T A=I, which is impossible when r<d. The stated full-SVD dimensions also make UV^T dimensionally invalid, although a reduced SVD could repair this. These issues directly affect reproducibility of a central component.

The claim that the CCA transformation preserves orthogonality of B is not generally true for arbitrary CCA projection and inverse-projection matrices. Moreover, the B-alignment formula in Eq. 21 differs from the formula in the main text and Algorithm 4. The theory establishes capacity for fixed orthogonal A and B, but does not establish that the proposed heterogeneous alignment produces aligned, orthogonal bases or reliable cross-model semantic correspondence.

Evidence specifically supporting SIMA is modest. In the principal component ablation, adding SIMA slightly decreases several Others metrics, while its gains over frozen-gradient aggregation in Table 20 are small relative to the reported variability. Thus, the broad claim that each component improves both personalization and generalization is stronger than the evidence.

The heterogeneous-model evaluation remains controlled: experiments involve at most three related LLaVA variants, generally sharing the same vision encoder and belonging to one language-model family per result table. Cross-family Llama-to-Qwen aggregation and genuinely different multimodal architectures are not directly evaluated, despite being central to the general heterogeneous-architecture motivation.

Experiments use only 5–10 clients and an infinite replay memory. Model assignments are selected using task-specific SFT performance rather than actual device constraints. These choices limit the realism of the claimed deployment setting and leave scalability of the N×N similarity computation and communication of last-layer gradients insufficiently studied.
SIMA communicates task gradients, but the paper does not analyze gradient leakage or otherwise reconcile this with its privacy motivation. No formal privacy protection is provided.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the benchmark and code are promised for release rather than supplied, several preprocessing and baseline-tuning choices are underspecified, and the pseudocode contains apparent errors such as testing i mod f instead of the iteration index. The limitations section acknowledges only the number of clients and omits these more consequential constraints.

strengths: FedMosaic addresses a practically important combination of task, temporal, and architectural heterogeneity that is insufficiently covered by much prior personalized federated learning work.

The proposed PQ-LoRA mechanism is an interesting and potentially useful approach for sharing compact parameters across models with different hidden dimensions and depths, while RELA provides client-specific aggregation based on estimated task relevance.
DRAKE is a substantial benchmark contribution, covering 40 multimodal tasks, 10 clients, temporal task shifts, multi-image inputs, and separate unseen-task evaluation.

The empirical study is unusually broad: it includes static and dynamic settings, homogeneous and heterogeneous clients, Llama- and Qwen-based models, cross-family configurations, up to 52 clients, multiple text-only benchmarks, three seeds, strong baselines, per-client results, cost analyses, and numerous sensitivity studies.

The principal results are consistent across configurations. FedMosaic generally improves personalization over local fine-tuning and substantially improves cross-client generalization, while reporting relatively modest communication and computation overhead.
weaknesses: The privacy claims are substantially stronger than the evidence. FedMosaic transmits gradients and model updates; EMA, coordinate subsampling, and Gaussian noise with an empirically selected scale do not establish privacy. There is no differential-privacy guarantee, privacy accounting, or evaluation against gradient-inversion or membership-inference attacks. Claims such as learning 'without privacy risks' and 'preserving privacy' should therefore be removed or qualified.

The theoretical treatment does not justify the central heterogeneous-model setting. The zero-aggregation-error result assumes identical frozen A and B matrices, which is impossible across models whose matrices have different dimensions. Saying that the argument 'easily extends' to heterogeneous models is unsupported, and there is no formal result showing that CCA/L2 alignment makes shared P and Q updates semantically compatible across architectures.

Some alignment details appear mathematically inconsistent or insufficiently specified. The paper claims that the CCA transformation preserves orthogonality without proof, uses inconsistent inverse/pseudoinverse notation, and presents an SVD post-processing expression whose stated full-matrix dimensions do not conform unless a thin SVD is implicitly assumed.

The ablations do not fully substantiate several causal claims. There is no RELA-only variant; adding RELA after PQ-LoRA slightly decreases one reported 'Others' endpoint metric, and the RELA ablation reports only 'Self' performance. Likewise, alignment gains are small relative to the reported variance, yet are described categorically.

Baseline comparability is imperfect because several methods are not natively designed for the heterogeneous setting and are combined with an additional aggregation method. More detail and ablation of these adaptations, along with comparisons to closely related heterogeneous-LoRA approaches when applicable, would strengthen the conclusions.

Evaluation and reproducibility details remain incomplete: open-ended-answer scoring is described only vaguely as comparison of 'correct tokens,' aggregation across differently sized tasks is unclear, no significance testing is provided, and the implementation and benchmark splits are only promised for future release. The reliance on GPT-based task construction/evaluation also warrants validation against human judgments.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored setting: personalized federated learning with simultaneous task, architecture, scale, and temporal heterogeneity.
DRAKE is potentially useful, combining 40 multimodal tasks from 19 datasets with multi-image inputs, temporal task sequences, and held-out adaptation tasks.
The empirical study is broad, covering Llama- and Qwen-based models, cross-family configurations, text-only benchmarks, three seeds, component ablations, and computational analyses.
The high-level ideas—task-relevance-weighted aggregation and sharing dimension-invariant low-rank modules—are intuitive and practically motivated.
weaknesses: The central PQ-LoRA alignment is not mathematically well specified. For A in R^{r×d}, the regularizer and constraint use A^T A=I, which is dimensionally inconsistent with I_r and generally impossible when r<d; the stated SVD solution instead produces row orthogonality. The CCA transformation also invokes an inverse of a generally rectangular projection matrix, and the appendix contradicts the main-text pseudoinverse formula. The claim that this transformation preserves B's orthogonality is unsupported and generally false.

The theory does not justify the main heterogeneous-model claim. The zero-aggregation-error theorem assumes identical frozen A and B matrices in a homogeneous setting, whereas heterogeneous clients have differently shaped, only approximately aligned matrices. Saying that the result “easily extends” does not establish that averaging P and Q has a consistent meaning across architectures.

The pseudocode is incomplete and internally inconsistent: the cross-architecture aggregation routine is undefined, conventional LoRA modules with incompatible dimensions appear to be included in aggregation, gradient frequency is indexed by client rather than iteration, and the loops seemingly execute R rounds for every task despite experiments reporting R total rounds. These issues prevent faithful reproduction of the claimed algorithm.

Privacy claims are substantially overstated. Federated learning does not inherently remove privacy risk, and EMA, coordinate subsampling, and Gaussian noise with an empirically chosen scale of 1e-4 provide no formal privacy guarantee. There is no differential-privacy accounting or empirical gradient-inversion evaluation, despite privacy preservation being repeatedly claimed.

The efficiency analysis appears to omit important costs, especially storing and running an additional 0.5B–1B relevance model on every client and the one-time public-data alignment. Gradient coordinates are subsampled after gradient computation in the pseudocode, so compression does not by itself support the claimed computation reduction. This undermines the resource-constrained-client motivation.

The evaluation omits especially relevant heterogeneous-LoRA baselines such as HETLORA and FLEXLORA, despite discussing them as the closest prior work. Several other baselines are modified through Fed-ET, but the exact adaptations and step-budget adjustments are insufficiently documented for assessing fairness.

The “realistic” dynamic setting uses infinite replay memory containing all prior samples, substantially weakening both the non-stationarity and resource-constrained-client premises. DRAKE is a curated reassignment of existing datasets to ten synthetic clients rather than evidence from naturally occurring federated populations.

Many headline personalization improvements over independent fine-tuning are modest, no statistical significance tests are supplied, and the strongest ablation for the novel alignment yields only small gains. Hyperparameters are selected on DRAKE-Dynamic and then much of the main evidence is reported on that same benchmark.

Reproducibility relies on a promise of future code and split release. Exact generated task partitions, dataset licenses, contamination controls, and implementation details needed to resolve the mathematical and pseudocode ambiguities are not presently available. Overall, the benchmark and empirical scope are promising, but the central method is not specified or validated soundly enough for acceptance.

strengths: Addresses an important and realistic problem: personalized federated learning with simultaneous task, temporal, model-size, and model-family heterogeneity.
FedMosaic combines two technically intuitive components: relevance-weighted client aggregation to reduce negative transfer and PQ-LoRA to share compact parameters across heterogeneous architectures.
DRAKE is a meaningful benchmark contribution, covering 40 multimodal tasks from 19 datasets, multi-image inputs, temporal task shifts, and separate unseen-task evaluation.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: static and dynamic settings, multimodal and text-only tasks, multiple model families and scales, up to 52 clients, three random seeds, strong PFL/distillation baselines, and supervised local fine-tuning.
Results are consistently favorable across the principal settings. Improvements are especially convincing for cross-client generalization, while most clients also improve in personalization.
The paper provides extensive component, alignment, hyperparameter, model-assignment, computational-cost, communication-cost, and fast-adaptation analyses.

The method appears practically attractive: reported computation is close to local fine-tuning, communication is reduced relative to transmitting full LoRA adapters, and a small or quantized relevance model remains effective.
Presentation is generally clear and the substantial appendix supplies implementation settings, client configurations, benchmark composition, pseudocode, and per-client results.
weaknesses: The theoretical support for PQ-LoRA under heterogeneous models is incomplete. The zero aggregation-error theorem assumes identical frozen A and B across clients, whereas heterogeneous architectures have dimensionally different A and B. The paper says the result extends easily, but does not establish an analogous notion of an ideal update or zero error across incompatible parameter spaces.

Some alignment arguments are technically questionable or underspecified. In particular, a generic CCA-based projection does not automatically preserve orthogonality as claimed, and the equations and pseudocode contain inconsistencies involving projection indices, pseudoinverses, layer indexing, gradient-update frequency, and the stated aggregation routine.

The privacy language is too strong. Sharing model updates and sanitized gradients does not make training free of privacy risks. Random coordinate subsampling and Gaussian noise with scale 1e-4 provide no formal differential-privacy guarantee, and the paper reports neither privacy accounting nor an empirical gradient-inversion evaluation.

Baseline fairness is not fully resolved. Methods are assigned local steps to equalize FLOPs with SFT, which can substantially reduce optimization for computationally heavier baselines. Results under matched rounds, local updates, or processed examples are needed alongside the fixed-compute comparison.

Several significance claims exceed the evidence. No statistical tests or confidence intervals are supplied, some improvements are small relative to reported standard deviations, the full alignment ablation has only marginal gains, and adding RELA slightly lowers the terminal Others score on DRAKE despite the claim that every component improves generalization.

The dynamic setting is a controlled four-task sequence with unlimited episodic memory and full replay. This weakens the claim that it closely represents realistic nonstationary clients, where storage, client availability, and participation are constrained.

DRAKE reuses and repartitions existing datasets, sometimes placing subsets from the same source on different clients. The paper lacks a systematic contamination/overlap audit against model pretraining data and does not fully discuss dataset licensing or redistribution constraints.

Reproducibility currently depends on a promised future release. Important construction details—exact sample identifiers, task-order generation, preprocessing, evaluation normalization, baseline-specific budgets, and GPT-based partitioning outputs—are not fully recoverable from the manuscript alone.

The main experiments involve only 9–10 fully participating multimodal clients; the 52-client result is text-only, while the claimed 1000-client scalability is based on cost extrapolation rather than end-to-end federated experiments. Robustness to partial participation, dropouts, and systems heterogeneity is untested.
